findings.title: [P1] Restore listener removal during cleanup
findings.body: When a consumer invokes the disposer returned by `attach`, the `"message"` handler now remains registered. Messages after teardown still invoke stale callbacks, and repeated attachment cycles accumulate listeners and duplicate processing.

findings.title: [P1] Clear the polling interval when stopped
findings.body: The returned stop function no longer cancels the interval. After teardown, `refresh` continues running indefinitely; repeated lifecycles accumulate work, and the active timer can prevent a Node.js process or test runner from exiting.

findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal in the returned disposer
findings.body:
After `attach()` registers a handler, invoking its returned cleanup function no longer removes it. Any socket message emitted afterward still calls stale handlers, causing duplicate processing and retaining associated state across reconnects or component teardown.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Cancel the interval when polling is stopped
findings.body:
Calling the function returned by `startPolling()` no longer stops the interval. The callback continues indefinitely after cancellation; in Node.js, the referenced interval also keeps the event loop alive, preventing normal process or test shutdown.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore socket unsubscription after teardown
findings.body:
The returned disposer no longer removes the message handler. On a long-lived or shared socket, a remote peer can send messages after session/component teardown and invoke stale handlers, potentially under obsolete authorization context; repeated attach/dispose cycles also amplify each message across retained handlers.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore interval cancellation to prevent resource exhaustion
findings.body:
Every polling interval now survives its advertised cleanup indefinitely. If polling lifecycles can be initiated repeatedly through requests, reconnects, or tenant sessions, an attacker can accumulate permanent callbacks and retained closure state, causing unbounded CPU/memory consumption and continued post-teardown activity.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Restore listener removal in the disposer
findings.body:
Calling the returned cleanup function no longer detaches the `"message"` handler. Any attach/dispose lifecycle retains the handler and its captured objects for the socket’s lifetime, continues invoking disposed consumers, and accumulates listeners across repeated attachments.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P2] Clear the polling interval during cleanup
findings.body:
Every `startPolling` call now creates an interval that cannot be stopped. After callers invoke the returned cleanup function, `refresh` still executes every second and remains retained; repeated lifecycles accumulate permanent work, and in Node.js the referenced timer can also prevent process termination.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Restore listener removal in the returned cleanup
findings.body:
Calling the disposer returned by `attach` no longer unregisters the `"message"` handler. Any consumer that detaches or is destroyed will continue receiving messages, causing stale callbacks, duplicate handling after reattachment, and listener leaks.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Clear the interval when polling is stopped
findings.body:
The returned stop function no longer cancels the interval. After consumers call it, `refresh` still executes every second indefinitely; in Node.js the live timer can also prevent process termination.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
